extracted.intended_audience: new college-level mathematics instructors / graduate teaching assistants
extracted.subtask_short: lesson planning for college math instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and a worksheet for planning interactive, student-centered lesson sessions in undergraduate mathematics; includes step-by-step meeting facilitation, lesson-planning steps, and example classroom activities using technology. Intended to help novice instructors generate and assess a concrete lesson plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the section to be covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, you will not need to read the section in as painstaking depth as you do your own textbooks, but it is very important that you know what topics are treated in the section and how the book treats them. You will plan your lesson under the assumption that your students have read the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the lesson assuming student pre-reading; familiarize yourself by planning a lesson using the worksheet to know what to expect students to have seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify learning objectives (3–5, student-centered and observable)
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the section, jot down the 3–5 main ideas the book presented and use them to formulate 3–5 student learning objectives. These objectives should state what bits of knowledge and what skills students should have acquired by the end of the lesson and should focus on the students' learning (not instructor-focused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State objectives so you can observe whether students achieved them; avoid instructor-centered phrasing (e.g., 'I will cover X') in favor of student-centered outcomes ('students will be able to...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide a strategy to address each goal (lecture, activity, or both)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each learning objective decide whether it will be best addressed through an instructor explanation (lecture), a student activity, or both. Mini-lectures can include student participation and activities often include instructor explication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an interplay between short mini-lectures and activities that foreshadow or solidify ideas; explicitly mark each goal with 'lecture', 'activity', or 'both'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management and chunking of lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify administrative items and allocate time; divide mini-lectures into 5- or 10-minute segments and do not lecture for more than 10 minutes at a time without switching gears. Subtract allocated lecture/admin time from total class time to find time remaining for activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a planning table for time allotted versus activities; communicate time frames clearly to students; factor in transition/setup/wrap-up times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan student activities (selection, grouping, and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an activity for each goal that requires one — e.g., textbook problems, worksheets, or instructor-designed tasks. Vary grouping (groups, pairs, individual) and decide how long to allocate to each activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate roughly two minutes each for setup and wrap-up of activities; break long or multipart problems into timed pieces (e.g., 4–5 minutes on parts (a),(b) then 2 minutes discussion), and plan group sizes appropriate to task difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution details for student activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan the particular execution of each activity: what you'll say to set it up, mechanics of forming groups and beginning work, how results are to be reported, what you will emphasize, and how the activity relates to other parts of the lesson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write explicit notes for setup instructions, reporting protocol, and key points to stress; anticipate logistical issues so group activities run smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write scripts for mini-lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose short scripts or note cards for each mini-lecture that anticipate student difficulties, move from concrete to abstract, plan board work (examples and graphs), prepare a higher-level question to ask, and plan transitions between lecture and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry concise scripts to class; explicitly plan anticipated stumbling points and how you will simplify language or give intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether learning objectives were met (in-class assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan brief, in-class assessment techniques to check whether the 3–5 learning objectives have been met by most students (e.g., calling on students, voting on answers, brief practice problems traded and checked, or collecting a 'minute paper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minute papers (summaries, 'muddiest point', or a short exercise) for end-of-class assessment; if objectives are not met, plan how to revisit the material or adjust future lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence the lesson and plan closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Write an outline of the order of the day's administration, mini-lectures, and activities, and plan how to wrap up the class period with a short summary of what was learned or a preview of upcoming reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit closing statements and next-step instructions; regular summarizing helps synthesize disparate activities into a coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-plan and contingency planning
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to over-plan than to under-plan. If you plan too much and cannot finish, assign unfinished activities as homework or resort to emergency lecturing; with experience you will learn appropriate pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have contingency plans (homework assignments, 'emergency lecture' topics) so time overruns do not compromise core objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting preparation logistics for instructor meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Before running the lesson-planning meeting: plan a lesson using the worksheet yourself, make enough copies of the worksheet and any questionnaires, ask instructors to read ahead in their textbooks and bring them, notify participants they're planning their next lesson, and circulate the agenda in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm attendance and prepare meeting materials in advance to ensure participants can produce realistic lesson plans during the session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitation and meeting-running procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested meeting flow: introduce the meeting (:01–:05), divide instructors into small groups to work through the worksheet (:05–:45), float around assisting groups, facilitate large-group discussions after major steps are mostly completed, and wrap up with summary or Q&A (:45–:50).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call attention to typical delicate aspects (identifying goals, strategies, and flow). Allow early finishers to leave if appropriate; use facilitator prompts to synthesize group responses into a broader discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use varied teaching methodologies to match cognitive processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mental processes are best facilitated by different kinds of student and instructor activities; therefore plan a variety of methodologies (mini-lectures, collaborative learning, student presentations, interactive questioning, writing) to achieve identified learning goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the methodology matched to the learning objective; do not rely solely on one method (e.g., pure lecture) when alternative activities better support the desired cognitive processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage cooperative learning and disruptive behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that mismanagement of cooperative learning activities and giving students partial control of class flow can lead to difficulties, including disruptive behavior and poor time management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan group management strategies (roles, reporting mechanisms) and refer to specific sections (e.g., Chapter 4 on cooperative learning and Chapter 9 on disruptive behavior) for tactics to prevent common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design extremal modeling activity (precalculus example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a real-world modeling problem (two islands and a shore station) that yields a distance-sum model D(x)=sqrt(x^2+1)+sqrt((4-x)^2+16) and have students use graphing calculators or computers to find the minimizing x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guide students to construct the model first, then use technology to explore and find the minimizer; emphasize modeling-to-technology workflow rather than purely symbolic solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure a Fourier-transform-based differential equation activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a differential equation (du/dt - u = e^{-t^2}), have students attempt a hand solution, prompt them about the Fourier transform relation of du/dt and u, use CAS to find Fourier transforms and inverse transforms, verify solutions with CAS differentiation commands, and combine with homogeneous solutions to produce the general solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a stepwise plan (attempt by hand, use transform properties, compute with CAS, verify solution, assemble general solution); example Maple commands provided (with(inttrans): fourier(exp(-t^2), t, omega); invfourier(1/(1+omega^2), omega, t);) to demonstrate practical CAS usage and limitations of manual inverse transforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate convergence of improper integrals using graphical, numeric, and algebraic approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphing calculators and computers to compute integrals (Riemann sums, integral commands, FTC), and graph functions (e.g., 1/x^2 and 1/sqrt(x)) over progressively large/small windows to compare tail behavior and area under curves. Connect graphical/numeric observations with algebraic results to determine convergence and examine vertical asymptote integrability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students experiment with different plotting windows (e.g., 0≤x≤0.01, 0≤x≤100000) and use trace/area estimation (e.g., fraction of viewing window) to build intuition about 'fat tails' vs rapidly decaying tails; then confirm with algebraic techniques which integrals converge and discuss counterexamples (tails that get thin but still give infinite area).
